title: Full-stack web roadmap
tagline: From a blank machine to a live app in six pages, with free Vietnamese videos.
intro: A path for complete beginners: six pages, one per part, read in order. Every video is free on YouTube and in Vietnamese, with F8 first.
This page is the map. Each page after it goes step by step, from setup to project, with tools current as of 11 October 2026.

sections.title: How to study
sections.summary: Read this first: how you study decides whether you finish the path.

blocks.caption: The loop of every lesson. Repeating it is the whole path.

items.label: Watch one lesson
items.detail: One 5–20 minute video, watched through once for the idea, no typing yet
explain: One lesson at a time. Watch five in a row and the first is gone before you type it.
1.25x is fine for talking, but drop back to 1x for the coding parts so you catch every character.

items.label: Close it, retype it
items.detail: Retype the code you just watched without looking, and run it to the same result
explain: This is where the learning happens. When you cannot recall it, reopen that bit, watch, close, then type on; never type while the video plays.
Type by hand, never paste. Your fingers need to learn the brackets, semicolons and function names.

items.label: Change one detail
items.detail: Change something small, guess the result first, then run it to check
explain: For example, switch justify-content from center to space-between, or map to filter. A right guess means you understand; a wrong one shows what to study.
Break a line on purpose to see what the error looks like. Next time a real one appears, you already know what it says.

items.label: Stuck? Search, then ask
items.detail: Read the error, search, ask an AI; after 30 minutes, ask a person
explain: Getting stuck is normal, even after years on the job. The skill to train is getting yourself unstuck, not never getting stuck.
Sitting alone with one error for over 30 minutes is a waste. Ask with the template below so others can help at once.

items.label: Commit and take notes
items.detail: End each session by pushing to GitHub and writing three things learned and one question
explain: Committing every session turns GitHub into a study diary: look back after a month and see how far you came.
The question written down today is often answered a few lessons later. If not, take it to someone.

rows: Windows 10/11 or macOS, 8 GB RAM, 20 GB free on an SSD
16 GB is more comfortable. Phones, tablets and Chromebooks will not do.
10–14 hours a week, ideally a little every day
Less still works, just longer than six months. Steadiness beats hours.
Read short sentences, looking words up as needed
Errors, docs and commands are all in English. Reading is enough; use a translator freely.
Basic computer use: download, install, find files
No maths needed. Web programming uses logic, not formulas.
Every tool in the path is free and needs no payment card.
Review yesterday: retype a piece of code you learned, without looking
Watch 2–3 new lessons using the loop above
Practise alone: exercises on f8.edu.vn, or part of the checklist project
Notes: three things learned, one open question
Commit, push, and mark your progress

items: Write in your own words, as if explaining to a friend who has not studied it. Copying the video's words does not help you remember.
Give each concept a short, runnable code example of your own.
Keep notes in a notes.md inside your study repo, committed with the code and searchable with Ctrl + F.
Record every error you hit and how you fixed it. That list becomes the most valuable document you write.
Read the error from start to end: it usually names the file, the line and the reason.
Print values with console.log just before the failing spot, and check they are what you think.
Search the exact error line plus the technology, such as "react" or "express". English results are usually more plentiful and newer.
Ask an AI with the code and the error, and ask why rather than just for fixed code.
Still stuck after 30 minutes? Ask a person, using the template below.
What you are doing: "I am building the sign-up form from lesson 80 of the basic JavaScript course."
What you expected: "Pressing Sign up shows an error under the email field."
What actually happened: paste the error word for word, never a summary.
What you tried: list each attempt and what it did.
The relevant code: pasted as text, only the part that matters; never a phone photo of the screen.
F8's Facebook group "Học lập trình web (fullstack.edu.vn)" and F8's Discord: full of people taking exactly these courses.
The comments under the video: someone has often asked your question already.
Stack Overflow: in English; search before asking, since most common errors are answered there.
A study partner: fixed sessions together and explaining lessons to each other is the surest way to remember.
Every page ends with a checklist: move on only when you can do all of it alone.
Write the start and finish date of each part in notes.md to see your progress.
In a busy week, drop to 30 minutes a day but never stop completely. One week off easily becomes quitting.
Weeks 3–4 are when the excitement usually fades. That is normal; pushing through it is the hardest part of the whole path.
Paste the error and the code around it, and ask why it fails. Ask for the reason, not just the fixed code.
Ask for a concept explained with a different example from the video, such as closures through a counter.
Write the checklist projects yourself. Letting AI write them skips exactly the part that makes you better.
Check answers against the official docs: MDN, react.dev, expressjs.com. AI may answer for an older version.
Turn off automatic code suggestions in VS Code until the end of part 3, so your hands learn the syntax.
Watching a whole course before coding: by then most of it is forgotten.
Moving to React with shaky JavaScript: every React bug after that is really a JavaScript bug.
Copying code from the video without understanding it: change one detail and you cannot fix it.
Taking several courses on one topic at once: pick one, finish it, then look elsewhere.
Comparing yourself with people online: everyone starts somewhere different. Compare only with yourself a month ago.

sections.title: Six parts
sections.summary: About 150 hours of video, and six months at two hours a day.

blocks.caption: Take them in order: each part builds on everything before it.

items.label: 1. Environment & tools
items.detail: Install a terminal, VS Code, Node.js and Git; learn how the web works
explain: Windows uses WSL to run Ubuntu inside the machine; macOS uses its own Terminal. From then on every command in the path is the same on both.
Node.js goes in through nvm, so switching versions is one command. On 11 October 2026 the LTS release is Node 24.
Git keeps the history of your code and GitHub keeps a copy online. Your first repo is pushed in this very part.

items.label: 2. HTML & CSS
items.detail: Build static pages, lay them out with flexbox, fit every screen
explain: HTML is the frame and CSS the dressing. F8's two projects, The Band and Shopee, take you from the first tag to a full shop page.
It ends with a page you build from a design image, published on GitHub Pages so you have a link to share.

items.label: 3. JavaScript
items.detail: Make pages respond: events, the DOM, calling APIs with fetch
explain: The longest and most important part: React and Node are both JavaScript, so every gap here shows up again later.
Three projects of your own: a to-do app, a validated sign-up form, and a weather app calling a real API.

items.label: 4. ReactJS
items.detail: Split the interface into components, hold data in hooks, change pages with a router
explain: Projects start with Vite instead of the video's Create React App. The page maps every place the old video differs from today's React 19.
The main project is F8's TikTok clone, built with Vite, with the config that replaces the video's customize-cra.

items.label: 5. Node, Express & MySQL
items.detail: Write a server, store data in MySQL, split code into MVC
explain: Express 5 answers requests by route; MySQL keeps the data. It covers installing MySQL on Windows (WSL) and macOS, and joining them with mysql2.
F8's Node video uses Express 4 and older libraries; a table shows each line to change so it runs on current versions.

items.label: 6. Full-stack & deploy
items.detail: A REST API, JWT sign-in, React on top, then online for free
explain: The backend returns JSON, React calls it, and sign-in uses bcrypt and JWT. This is the project for your CV.
Free deployment: MySQL on Aiven, the backend on Render, the frontend on Vercel, step by step with each free plan's limits.

body: Times assume two hours a day, with an hour of your own coding for every hour of video. Going slower is fine; skipping the coding is not.

rows: Your first repo is on GitHub
A responsive landing page on GitHub Pages
A to-do app, sign-up form and weather app work
The to-do app rebuilt in React, with a router
An MVC Express server reading and writing MySQL
An app of your own with sign-in and a live link

sections.title: Portfolio & job hunting
sections.summary: Employers look at what you built, not at the courses you took.

items: Three projects with live links: a landing page, a React app, a full-stack app
Every repo has a README: a screenshot, features, stack, how to run it
At least one project of your own idea, not a clone from a video
A one-page CV: skills, the three projects with links, and your GitHub
